handbookNote: Massachusetts Notary Public Law -- compiled directly from official primary sources, not an AI summary or secondary aggregator (no NNA material used). Full compiled source text saved at temp/handbooks/ma/notary.txt. SOURCE CORRECTION -- IMPORTANT: this track's build brief assumed Massachusetts notary standards are governed primarily by 'Executive Order 455: Standards for the Office of Notary Public,' with instructions to fetch it directly from mass.gov. Direct research shows that premise is now out of date. The URL https://www.mass.gov/executive-orders/no-455-standards-for-the-office-of-notary-public returns a live 404 ('Not found') on mass.gov as of the build date. Mass.gov's own current official guidance page ('Becoming a Notary Public') states verbatim that 'On January 4, 2017 a new law governing standards of conduct for notaries public went into effect... all notaries public... must comply with Chapter 222 of the General Laws as amended by Chapter 289 of the Acts of 2016' -- citing ONLY the statute, never EO 455. The official 2025 notary application itself has the applicant attest to having read 'Chapter 222 of the General Laws, as amended by Chapter 289 of the Acts of 2016' -- again, statute only. None of the 27 active sections of M.G.L. c. 222 reference EO 455. CONCLUSION: Massachusetts notary standards are now governed primarily by STATUTE -- M.G.L. c. 222 ('Justices of the Peace, Notaries Public and Commissioners'), comprehensively rewritten by Chapter 289 of the Acts of 2016 (effective Jan 4, 2017) -- not by a currently-live executive order. The Governor retains the constitutional appointing/commissioning role (Article IV of the Amendments; discretion to deny/revoke under sections 13 and 26 of c.222), but the conduct rules themselves are codified in statute. This correction is documented here for institutional memory since it differs from the task's original premise. CLASSIFICATION CONFIRMATION: Massachusetts is a genuine application-only notary state for the BASE commission -- confirmed independently, not assumed. No exam of any kind (written, oral, or proctored) appears anywhere in M.G.L. c. 222, the mass.gov guidance pages, or the official 2025 application form. No pre-commission training or education course is required for the base commission. No surety bond is required -- confirmed by the complete absence of any bond provision in c.222 or the application materials (the task's own steering note suspected this and it is now verified firsthand rather than assumed). Fee is $60, paid to the Secretary of the Commonwealth only AFTER the Governor and Governor's Council approve the application (never submitted with it). Term is 7 years (c.222 sec.14). Qualifications are age 18+ and Massachusetts residency or regular place of work/business (sec.13(a)); denial/revocation are matters of gubernatorial discretion under specific statutory grounds (sec.13(b), sec.26). NOTABLE QUIRK 1 -- FOUR CHARACTER REFERENCES, ONE MUST BE AN ATTORNEY: the official application requires four references who personally know the applicant and attest under penalties of perjury to the applicant's 'high standing and character' -- and per the form, one of the four must be 'a member of the bar in good standing.' This attorney-reference requirement is distinctive among the application-only states built so far in this batch. NOTABLE QUIRK 2 -- GOVERNOR AND GOVERNOR'S COUNCIL APPOINT, NOT AN AGENCY: the petition is literally addressed 'To Her Excellency the Governor,' reflecting Massachusetts's unique constitutional structure (Article IV of the Amendments; the Governor's Council is itself a separate elected constitutional body that must consent to commissions and revocations). NOTABLE QUIRK 3 -- REMOTE/ELECTRONIC NOTARIZATION IS A SEPARATE, CLEARLY-LABELED SUB-MODULE WITH ITS OWN POSSIBLE TRAINING REQUIREMENT: c.222 secs.27-29 create an opt-in 'communication technology' (remote online notarization) framework. A notary who wants to notarize for remotely-located individuals must separately register with the Secretary of the Commonwealth, and -- per sec.28(n) -- the Secretary MAY require completion of an in-person or online training course on remote-notarization duties/technology before the notary's first remote act, capped by statute at 3 hours. This mirrors the 'separate endorsement with its own training/exam requirement' pattern seen elsewhere in this batch (e.g., Kansas, South Carolina) -- except in Massachusetts it is a conditional training course, not an exam, and it applies only to the optional remote-notarization endorsement, never to the base commission. This track builds that material as a clearly separate topic bucket ('Remote and Electronic Notarization') rather than folding it into the general no-exam framing. NOTABLE QUIRK 4 -- THE ONLY STATUTORY NOTARY 'FEE SCHEDULE' IS NARROW AND HISTORICAL: c.222 repeatedly cross-references 'the maximum fees provided in section 41 of chapter 262' as the fee cap for notarial acts -- but that statute (c.262 sec.41) actually sets fees only for protesting negotiable instruments (bills of exchange, drafts, checks, promissory notes), a narrow and largely historical notarial function. There is no separate General Laws price schedule for common acts like acknowledgments or jurats; those are left to market rates subject to the anti-overcharging language in sec.16(a)(vi). This nuance is tested directly and documented for institutional memory. CONTENT DEPTH: M.G.L. c. 222 is unusually rich for an application-only state -- 27 active substantive sections (2 formally repealed) covering 27 defined terms, appointment/jurisdiction, out-of-state/foreign commissioners, oath/seal rules, expiration penalties, records-destruction penalties, military acknowledgments, journal exemptions, qualifications/7 denial grounds, 7-year term, five distinct statutory notarial-act certificate forms (acknowledgment/jurat/signature-witnessing/copy-certification/signature-by-mark/signing-for-the-physically-unable), an 11-clause prohibited-acts list plus a 4-exception duty-to-serve provision, attorney-practice-of-law and immigration-services boundaries (cross-referencing c.221 sec.46E's real-estate-closing rules), tiered criminal/civil penalties and a private right of action under c.93A, detailed 9-part journal-keeping rules, narrow fee exemptions, seal/record destruction on expiration, 10-day change-of-address notice, revocation standards, tamper-evident e-notarization technology, and a very detailed 16-subsection remote-notarization framework (sec.28) plus a personal-information-use restriction (sec.29). This depth is comparable to several of the richer states already built in this batch, despite having no exam/training/bond for the base commission. QUESTION BANK: 182 grounded questions were generated across 11 topic buckets (Definitions and Key Terms; Notarial Acts and Authority; Certificates and Notarial Forms; Seals, Stamps and Electronic Signatures; Commissioning, Qualifications and Application; Prohibited Acts and Duty to Serve; Practice of Law, Immigration and Real Estate Closings; Journal Requirements; Discipline, Penalties and Revocation; Notary Fees; and Remote and Electronic Notarization as a clearly separate module) -- every question cites a specific M.G.L. c.222 section (or the cross-referenced c.262 sec.41 / c.221 sec.46E, or the official mass.gov application materials) and is grounded in the verbatim fetched text; no padding, invented facts, or filler was used to hit a target ('better nothing than nonsense' per the site owner's standing directive).
